Two‐stage spatiotemporal graph neural network framework for seizure onset zone localization
nodes.venue: Epilepsia
nodes.abstract: Abstract Objective Accurate localization of the seizure onset zone (SOZ) is critical for the presurgical evaluation of drug‐resistant epilepsy. Intracranial electroencephalography captures high‐resolution seizure dynamics, but interpreting complex spatiotemporal patterns across implanted electrodes is clinically challenging. We propose a two‐stage, uncertainty‐aware framework for SOZ localization that integrates patient‐specific seizure modeling with cross‐patient probabilistic ranking to estimate the likelihood of each electrode belonging to the SOZ. Methods The framework was evaluated on a bi‐institutional cohort of 36 patients (20 with good surgical outcome, 16 with poor surgical outcome), comprising 184 seizures. In the first stage, a patient‐specific spatiotemporal graph neural network modeled seizure onset as a network‐level transition using directed functional connectivity graphs derived from burst‐integrated electrophysiological features. Trained solely to detect preictal‐to‐ictal transitions, this model generated electrode probability trajectories without SOZ supervision. In the second stage, these trajectories were summarized into interpretable descriptors and used to train a patient‐agnostic classifier assigning SOZ likelihood scores to electrodes. Evaluation and hyperparameter optimization were performed using nested leave‐one‐patient‐out cross‐validation restricted to good outcome patients, ensuring strict patient‐level separation between training, validation, and test data. Results Seizure onset detection was stable across patients, with comparable binary cross‐entropy values between outcome groups (median = .495 vs. .438, p = .108). In good outcome patients, SOZ electrodes were prioritized among top‐ranked contacts (area under the curve = .86 ± .06), with all patients exhibiting at least one SOZ electrode within the top positions. In poor outcome patients, predictions exhibited reduced spatial separability, lower likelihood magnitudes, and near‐zero confidence gaps, reflecting attenuated model confidence. Significance This two‐stage framework integrates spatial interactions, temporal dynamics, and probabilistic ranking within a pipeline. By providing graded SOZ likelihood estimates and uncertainty‐aware prioritization, the approach is a decision‐support tool to assist hypothesis refinement during presurgical evaluation rather than as a standalone diagnostic system.

nodes.name: The influence of sample size, modelling algorithms, and hyperparameters on bootstrap-based prediction stability in clinical prediction model development: An empirical study using the HOPE dataset
nodes.venue: BMC Medical Research Methodology
nodes.abstract: Abstract Background The stability of clinical prediction models has emerged as an important factor in model development. Models producing unstable or unreliable predictions can ultimately lead to improper clinical decisions and harm patients when applied in clinical practice. Previous studies have highlighted the role of sample size in prediction stability, with larger samples delivering increased stability. However, the role of other modelling decisions remains unclear. This study considered three modifiable factors influencing the stability of predictions: sample size, modelling algorithm (i.e., parametric regression and machine learning algorithms), and hyperparameter tuning. Methods We used the previously published HOPE dataset to develop a prediction model for anxiety at palliative care admission, incorporating 34 candidate predictors. To examine the impact of sample size, we generated seven datasets of varying sizes through random sampling. A total of 21 modelling scenarios were evaluated by combining these datasets with three modelling approaches: LASSO logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost. Models were tuned using cross-validation and assessed for discrimination (AUC) and calibration. Prediction stability was evaluated using a bootstrap-based framework, including the mean absolute prediction error (MAPE) and related instability plots. Results In this clinical dataset, larger sample sizes were associated with lower average MAPE and a higher proportion of predictions with MAPE ≤ 5% for LASSO, with limited additional changes beyond the reference size ( n = 3,875). LASSO also showed lower AUC optimism and calibration slopes closer to 1 across increasing sample sizes. Random forest and XGBoost showed higher discrimination than LASSO in some scenarios, but had higher average MAPE, a lower proportion of predictions with MAPE ≤5%, and calibration slopes further from 1 across sample sizes. Conservative hyperparameter settings, such as shallower trees and slower learning rates, were associated with lower MAPE but slightly lower discrimination. Conclusions Our results provide empirical insights into bootstrap-based prediction stability in clinical prediction model development. Model stability appeared to depend not only on sample size but also on modelling approach and hyperparameter tuning. For machine learning models, considering stability alongside marginal gains in accuracy may be important. Further research should explore alternative validation strategies and optimal tuning practices to guide robust clinical prediction model development.

nodes.name: Strategic Location and Survival Dynamics of Businesses in San Diego County: A Comparative Machine Learning and Geospatial Approach
nodes.abstract: Background: Municipal business registries provide valuable information for examining business conditions and characteristics associated with longevity. However, recorded business-status fields do not necessarily contain complete event histories required for formal survival analysis. This study therefore examines recorded active and closed/canceled business status rather than time-to-event survival probabilities.Purpose: This study compares logistic regression with four tree-based ensemble classifiers to distinguish recorded business status among San Diego County establishments. SHAP interpretation and unsupervised clustering are also used to examine structural and geographic patterns.Methods: The integrated dataset contained 158,330 initial records and 140,737 establishments after cleaning. The supervised modeling dataset included 137,814 observations after excluding 2,923 records without valid geographic coordinates. A stratified 80/20 split produced 110,251 training and 27,563 holdout test observations. SMOTE was applied exclusively to the training data, balancing both classes at 69,998 observations each. Five classifiers were evaluated on the same unaltered holdout set. SHAP was used to interpret LightGBM predictions, while K-Prototypes (k = 4) and spatial K-Means (k = 7) characterized business profiles and geographic patterns.Results: Logistic regression achieved an F1-score of 0.587087, accuracy of 0.661834, and ROC-AUC of 0.683970. LightGBM achieved the highest accuracy (0.835679), recall (0.760220), F1-score (0.792553), and ROC-AUC (0.911295). XGBoost achieved the highest precision (0.829190). SHAP identified business age as the strongest contributor to LightGBM predictions, followed by ownership, density, geographic, and industry features. Clustering identified distinct business profiles and spatial concentrations.Conclusions: Ensemble classifiers outperformed the logistic-regression baseline on the holdout dataset. Business age and ownership structure contributed substantially to model predictions. These findings represent associations with recorded business status, not causal effects or direct estimates of survival over time. Future research using longitudinal records and verified opening and closure dates could extend this framework to formal survival analysis.Keywords: Business Status Classification; Business Survival; Machine Learning; LightGBM; SHAP; Spatial Analysis; Business Clustering; San Diego County.

nodes.name: Probing EEG Foundation Model Attention Maps for Lightweight Interpretable Emotion Recognition
nodes.abstract: Foundation Models (FMs) trained on EEG signals promise subject- and dataset-independent pipelines for brain-computer interface (BCI) applications, but have yet to consistently outperform task-specific architectures, and their large representations are costly to compute and store. As a means of advancing the understanding of the Foundation Models' inner mechanisms, we propose a lightweight alternative that exploits the self-attention mechanism of REVE, a pretrained EEG FM, to derive features similar to weighted Functional Connectivity (FC) without any fine-tuning. Inspired by kernel-based FC matrices, we aggregate the raw first-layer attention weights of a single head over the full duration of dataset trials into weighted channel-to-channel adjacency matrices. These matrices replace standard encoder representation vectors as classification features, substantially reducing computational cost. We further introduce a label-free, symmetry-based criterion, motivated by the emergence of near-symmetric attention patterns in trained encoder-decoder transformers, ranking attention heads by how much discriminative information they carry. Classical machine learning classifiers are then trained on the single most informative head's attention-derived FC matrix and achieve balanced accuracy and F1 scores on the SEED-IV emotion-recognition dataset that are competitive with several fully fine-tuned state-of-the-art EEG Foundation Models, requiring at least two orders of magnitude fewer calculations than the standard use of the encoder. Subsequent cortical region analysis revealed a significant over-representation of frontal region connections by ranking the most discriminative FC matrix connectivity edges, validating our methods as consistent with prior affective-computing literature. These results suggest that interpretable, computationally inexpensive linear probing of attention maps is a viable route to deploying EEG Foundation Models in resource-constrained settings.

nodes.name: Predicting economies of scale in Brazilian municipal expenditure: Panel econometrics and interpretable machine learning
nodes.venue: Environment and Planning B: Urban Analytics and City Science
nodes.abstract: Municipal size is a persistent question in urban planning and public finance because small jurisdictions may face high per capita costs, whereas larger jurisdictions may face congestion and administrative complexity. This study compares panel econometric and interpretable machine-learning models for real municipal operational expenditure per capita in Brazil. The analysis uses 49,228 municipality-year observations for 5,568 municipalities from 2013 to 2021 and evaluates prediction through municipality-holdout, temporal-holdout, and state-block designs. Histogram Gradient Boosting performs best for unseen municipalities and held-out states, while a municipality fixed-effects-style predictor performs best for later-year prediction of municipalities already observed in the panel. The results indicate strong economies of scale among small municipalities followed by a broad low-cost range rather than one universal optimum. Controlled econometric and spatial-error models imply minima near 143,000 to 176,000 residents, while a reduced-form pooled OLS model excluding grants implies about 232,000 residents. The strongest boosting models show no clear interior upturn within the evaluated grid, with predicted expenditure remaining within 10% of the minimum above approximately 48,000 to 53,000 residents. Grouped SHAP results rank population first, followed by grants and local economic capacity. Residual Moran tests show that unexplained expenditure differences remain spatially clustered. The findings support spatially informed expenditure benchmarking and caution against consolidation policies based on one fixed population threshold.

Multiplex Determination of Pathogens via a Dual-Mode Microfluidic Platform Integrated with a Universal Sensing Strategy
nodes.venue: Analytical Chemistry
nodes.abstract: Abstract Multiplex determination of pathogens is crucial for precise medical treatment of infectious diseases. To address this challenge, here we propose a CRISPR/Cas-assisted microfluidic multiplex sensing platform (CAMMSP) based on a nucleic acid amplification-free, universal, and modular sensing strategy. This strategy leverages the synergistic action of Cas12a and nanoporous materials to construct a target-responsive indicator release/enrichment system and achieve cascade signal amplification without nucleic acid amplification. By virtue of the programmability of the CRISPR system, this strategy is readily extended to different targets by replacing crRNA only. With the aid of a spatially divisional microfluidic platform, four common reproductive tract pathogens were synchronously detected as a proof-of-concept. The signal property of the methylene blue indicator was utilized to achieve electrochemical and optical signal cross-validation, guaranteeing the detection reliability at the readout level and offering flexible options for different scenarios. The developed CAMMSP exhibits broad linear ranges across 6 orders of magnitude and sub-femtomolar detection limits, with outstanding specificity in complex samples. Clinical sample analysis further validates its potential for practical applications, establishing a promising laboratory proof-of-concept and reliable technical foundation for developing multiplex point-of-care testing devices.

nodes.name: Multimodal Emotion Detection in Distributed Data Streams: Deep Transformer Ensembles, Cross-Modal Attention Fusion, and Benchmark Evaluation
nodes.venue: International Journal of Creative and Open Research in Engineering and Management
nodes.abstract: Emotion detection represents a vital frontier at the inter-section of affective computing, artificial intelligence, and human-computer interaction (HCI). While traditional uni-modal systems—relying solely on text, speech acoustics, or static facial photographs—have established founda-tional benchmarks, they remain fundamentally fragile in real-world conversational dialogues characterized by lex-ical ambiguity, acoustic sarcasm, and visual occlusions. In this paper, we propose an end-to-end, publication-grade deep learning architecture for Multimodal Emo-tion Detection in Distributed Big Data Streams. Our framework synchronizes three specialized foundation models: a linguistic contextual transformer (RoBERTa-Large), a self-supervised acoustic representation encoder (Wav2Vec 2.0), and a spatiotemporal Vision Transformer (ViT-B/16) integrated with Facial Action Unit (FAU) tracking. To resolve temporal granularity discrepancies and inter-modal information imbalance, we formulate a novel Hierarchical Cross-Modal Attention Fusion (HCAF) network. The HCAF module leverages bidirec-tional multi-head cross-attention to project acoustic and vi-sual features into the linguistic latent subspace, selectively attending to emotional cues across communicative chan-nels. To address severe affective class skew (where neutral utterances dominate dialogue corpora), we design a hy-brid multi-task loss combining Focal Loss (γ = 2.0) with Concordance Correlation Coefficient (CCC) optimization for continuous Valence-Arousal dimensional estimation. Furthermore, we architect a distributed stream ingestion pipeline capable of sustaining over 450 concurrent mul-timodal streams per GPU node with sub-50ms latency, incorporating biometric facial landmark de-identification and vocal tract perturbation to guarantee user privacy under GDPR Article 9. We perform extensive empirical evaluations on the Multimodal EmotionLines Dataset (MELD) and the Interactive Emotional Dyadic Mo-tion Capture (IEMOCAP) corpus. Our HCAF model achieves a weighted F1-score of 71.6% on MELD (7-class) and 82.3% on IEMOCAP (4-class), outperforming uni-modal text, audio, and visual baselines by 7.7%, 27.5%, and 30.8% respectively, while surpassing standard Early and Late fusion paradigms by 5.9% and 4.6%. Ablation experiments and Pareto latency analyses confirm that cross-modal self-attention and dynamic loss re-weighting are crucial for robust, real-time affective computing. Keywords: Affective Computing, Multimodal Emotion Recognition, Vision Transformer, Wav2Vec 2.0, RoBERTa, Cross-Attention Fusion, Focal Loss, Distributed Stream Analytics, Biometric Privacy Preservation.

nodes.name: International Journal of Creative and Open Research in Engineering and Management
MultiSHAP: a Shapley-based framework for explaining cross-modal interactions in multimodal AI models
nodes.venue: npj Artificial Intelligence
nodes.abstract: Abstract Multimodal AI models have achieved impressive performance in tasks that require integrating information from multiple modalities, such as vision and language. While existing model explanation methods, such as attention maps and Grad-CAM, offer insights into cross-modal relationships, they do not explicitly quantify fine-grained interactions between individual visual and textual elements and require access to model internals. Here we introduce MultiSHAP, an architecture-agnostic interpretability framework that leverages the Shapley Interaction Index to attribute multimodal outputs to pairwise interactions between fine-grained visual and textual elements, such as image patches and text tokens. MultiSHAP does not require access to model parameters, gradients, attention weights, or intermediate representations, but requires a query interface that permits separate perturbation of visual and textual inputs and returns a task-relevant scalar score, either directly or through a ranked output from which such a score can be deterministically constructed. Our approach provides: (1) instance-level explanations that characterize how specific visual and textual elements jointly affect a selected model output, and (2) dataset-level descriptive summaries of interaction patterns under a specified model, value function, feature partition, and masking operator. Experiments on multimodal benchmarks provide evidence that MultiSHAP captures behaviorally relevant input-level interactions, while pair-level evaluations provide partial evidence that the estimated patch–token correspondences contain information beyond unimodal saliency, and case studies illustrate its use for examining individual multimodal decisions. Although evaluated here on vision–language models, the underlying interaction formulation may in principle be extended to other modality combinations.

nodes.name: LEARNING PREFERENCE PATTERNS AMONG 1ST-YEAR MBBS STUDENTS USING THE VISUAL, AURAL, READ/WRITE AND KINESTHETIC FRAMEWORK: A CROSS-SECTIONAL STUDY
nodes.venue: Asian Journal of Pharmaceutical and Clinical Research
nodes.abstract: Objective: Mapping learning preferences at entry into the MBBS course may help faculty design teaching sessions that are more responsive to learner diversity.The present study aims to evaluate the VARK learning preferences among first-year MBBS students. Methods: This cross-sectional questionnaire-based study was conducted among 235 first-year MBBS students The VARK questionnaire version 8.02 was administered using an online Google Form. The data was analysed using descriptive statistics, Chi-square/Fisher’s exact test, Mann–Whitney U test, Friedman test and Spearman’s correlation. Results: Of the 238 students recorded, 164 (68.9%) were females and 74 (31.1%) were males. The mean age was 19.30±1.41 years. Complete VARK data were available for 235 students. Multimodal learning was predominant [157/235 (66.8%)], with bimodal learning being the single most frequent mode [85/235 (36.2%)]. The distribution of learning modes did not differ significantly by gender (p=0.983). The highest mean component score was observed for Kinesthetic learning (8.98±3.89), followed closely by Aural learning (8.83±3.86), and the four VARK component scores differed significantly within participants (p<0.001). The most frequent specific learning preference was Aural-Kinesthetic [42/235 (17.9%)]. Among unimodal learners, Kinesthetic preference was dominant [37/78 (47.4%)]. Older students aged 20-22 years showed higher Visual (p=0.009) and Read/Write scores (p=0.018) than those aged 18-19 years. Spearman analysis showed the strongest positive correlation between Visual and Read/Write scores (p<0.001). Conclusion: First-year MBBS students demonstrated predominantly multimodal learning preferences, with a strong kinesthetic and aural orientation. Knowledge-enhanced named entity recognition for cyber threat intelligence: a multi-stage classification and retrieval framework
nodes.venue: Journal of Computer Virology and Hacking Techniques
nodes.abstract: Abstract Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) increasingly appears as unstructured text across social media and open-source security reports, yet its volume and noise make timely, accurate extraction a persistent bottleneck for defenders. We present a multi-stage CTI processing framework that couples domain-specific classification with knowledge-enhanced Named Entity Recognition (NER). A classifier fine-tuned from SecureBERT, a cybersecurity-specific language model, first filters threat-relevant content, achieving 92.41% accuracy and a 93.36% F1-score on a public CTI classification corpus and achieving the highest observed performance for Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest (RF), and the larger general-domain DeBERTa-Large baselines trained under matched conditions. A knowledge retrieval module then augments candidate text with external context drawn from Wikipedia and Wikidata using three Best Matching 25 (BM25) strategies: sparse Wikipedia retrieval, sparse Wikidata retrieval, and Wikidata entity-attribute lookup. Evaluated on the DNRTI benchmark with a SecureBERT encoder coupled to a Conditional Random Field (CRF) layer, knowledge augmentation raises entity-level F1 from 87.16% (no retrieval) to 93.01%, attaining the highest recall (93.44%) and F1-score among reported methods; the gains are most pronounced for proper-noun entity types such as hacker organisations and affected geographic areas, where external descriptions resolve aliases and ambiguity. We analyse each retrieval strategy, report category-level results, and candidly delineate the framework’s limitations, including the report-versus-tweet domain gap, English-only coverage, and the absence of statistical significance testing. Overall, the study shows that pairing a domain-adapted encoder with lightweight external knowledge retrieval is an effective and computationally economical route to improving CTI extraction.

Investigating urban development using remote sensing and GIS techniques (A case study: Sheberghan city (2005-2024)
nodes.venue: Kabul Polytechnic University International Journal of Engineering & Technology
nodes.abstract: The present study aimed to investigate the trend of spatial changes in land use in Sheberghan city during the period 2005 to 2024. This study, using remote sensing (RS) technology and geographic information system (GIS), analyzed the changes in land cover and different land uses in detail. For this purpose, Landsat satellite images from 2005, 2014, and 2024 were used, and after data preprocessing, supervised classification was performed using the Random Forest algorithm. The NDBI and NDVI indices were also used to examine regional changes. The research findings show that over the past two decades, Sheberghan city has faced a significant expansion of built-up areas and a decrease in natural lands such as agricultural lands, vegetation, and bare soils. The most significant changes have occurred in the central and eastern areas of the city, which indicates unplanned urban development and increased population pressure on natural resources. Also, the classification accuracy was higher in classes such as buildings and trees, while it was lower in the road and agricultural land classes. The results of this research can be used in urban planning, natural resource management, preparation of sustainable development plans and a regular urban plan for urban development in Sheberghan city.

nodes.name: Emergence of Spatial Structure From a Logical Substrate
nodes.venue: IPI Letters
nodes.abstract: This work shows how the kinematic framework of a quantum geometry follows from a logical substrate, and bounds by two no-go theorems what cannot follow from it. It does not propose a competing theory of quantum gravity: the group, the state space and the unit of horizon counting, one bit per face, are obtained here from the substrate. The value of the Immirzi parameter requires a horizon, hence the next levels. The minimal grain has four configurations, realised as two binary distinctions. A toggle and a conditional operation do not commute. Their commutators generate a Lie algebra of dimension three, isomorphic to that of rotations, in which the three dimensions of space are read (an interpretation). Under an information criterion, the grain has four legs. On an arena chosen by comparison, not by classification, the grains tile space with identical tetrahedra, whose angles close exactly around every edge: space is flat, and the tiling is bipartite. Under stated premises, the signature of spacetime cannot be derived at this level, no root of minus one is chosen, and there is no dynamics.The concept of the programme is posited before any computation, The seven reading rules formulated knowing their targets follow from it, and so does the Born rule. A single coupling governs the network. Beyond a threshold it orders into a vacuum, and the balance between the complexity of its exchanges and its capital, the entropy of its configurations, which measures durability, places the coupling in a zone just above the threshold. This vacuum is not critical: the continuum is an effective description of it, isotropic up to fourth order. On this vacuum, the three pairings of the grain are read as three families, and, under a postulate on its modes, a node with one extra leg gives the sixteen states of a generation. The level fixes ranges, not values. The eighteen computed mass ratios and mixing angles fall within their ranges, up to the measurement error; these are agreements, not predictions. With the measured mass splitting, the sum of neutrino masses lies between 0.063 and 0.070 electronvolt, straddling the current cosmological bound, and the violation of charge–parity symmetry by leptons has the sign opposite to that of the quarks, a refutable consequence of the framework. The compromise between accumulating and multiplying links fixes the form of the gauge action with no free parameter, and the coupling at the grain falls within the value required by the measured couplings run to unification. Fine values settle at the next levels. Seven structures are missing at this level; a single new choice at the next level would lift them, together with results already acquired; that it is the only remedy is a conjecture. Every statement carries its status.

nodes.name: Development of a Maintenance Management Cost-Effectiveness Prediction Model for Ageing Bridge Infrastructure: A Case of TARURA, Tanga Region, Tanzania
nodes.venue: East African Journal of Engineering
nodes.abstract: Bridges managed by the Tanzania Rural and Urban Roads Agency (TARURA) in Tanga Region are maintained largely reactively. About 78% of the annual bridge maintenance budget of TZS 850 million is spent on emergency repairs that cost 2.5 to 4 times more than equivalent preventive work. Existing bridge prediction models mostly predict condition rather than cost, require long inspection histories or large datasets, and omit institutional factors such as budget adequacy. This study therefore developed a maintenance management cost-effectiveness prediction model for ageing bridges in Tanga Region. It adopted a pragmatic philosophy and a convergent parallel mixed-methods design within a single case study of TARURA Tanga. Data were collected through document review, field observation and a structured questionnaire administered to 80 TARURA staff and contractors selected by stratified random and purposive sampling. Factors were ranked with the Relative Importance Index (RII). A multiple linear regression (MLR) model of annual maintenance cost was then estimated from the records of 80 bridges and benchmarked against a Random Forest. Seven of fourteen candidate factors met the RII threshold of 0.74, led by budget adequacy and allocation methods (0.970) and coastal exposure and corrosion (0.945). On a hold-out test set, the MLR achieved R² = 0.833 and MAPE = 13.0%, outperforming the Random Forest (R² = 0.517, MAPE = 22.5%). Structural age had the largest cost-increasing effect, and treatment selection had the largest cost-reducing effect. Each one-level improvement across all seven factors lowered predicted annual cost by about TZS 2.43 million per bridge. The study concludes that institutional factors drive bridge maintenance cost alongside physical deterioration. It also concludes that a transparent model built on routine inspection data can rank interventions by cost-effectiveness under a fixed budget. It recommends that TARURA Tanga shift funds from emergency to preventive maintenance and prioritise corrosion protection for coastal bridges and axle-load control on agricultural routes. It further recommends standardising inspection records to capture the model inputs and adopting the model as a spreadsheet decision tool until a computerised Bridge Management System is developed.

nodes.name: CT radiomics combined with 3D deep learning interpretable model to predict the efficacy of PD-1 inhibitor plus platinum-based chemotherapy in advanced NSCLC: a three-center retrospective cohort study
nodes.abstract: Abstract Background Platinum‑based chemotherapy combined with PD‑1 inhibitors serves as standard systemic treatment for unresectable stage IIIB–IV non‑small‑cell lung cancer (NSCLC) in both first‑line and later‑line settings; however, primary resistance causes substantial treatment‑response heterogeneity. Tissue‑based biomarkers including PD‑L1 expression and tumor mutational burden (TMB) are limited by invasive biopsy requirements and high costs, whereas routine thin‑slice chest CT non‑invasively captures intratumoral spatial heterogeneity. We constructed a multimodal interpretable AI model integrating clinical variables, three‑dimensional (3D) radiomics and pre‑trained 3D‑DenseNet latent features to predict immunochemotherapy response and evaluate its cross‑center generalizability. Methods We retrospectively enrolled 378 advanced NSCLC patients receiving PD‑1 inhibitor plus platinum‑based chemotherapy from three tertiary hospitals. Three‑dimensional regions of interest (ROIs) of primary tumors were manually double‑blinded segmented. Following three‑step feature filtering, four models were built: clinical‑only, radiomics‑only, standalone 3D deep learning (DL), and multimodal fusion. Center 1 data were split into training (n = 66) and internal validation (n = 35) sets; Centers 2 and 3 formed two fully independent external test sets (n = 81 and n = 196). Model performance was evaluated via area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and decision curve analysis (DCA). Ablation, multi‑classifier and subgroup analyses assessed robustness. SHAP and 3D Grad‑CAM enabled model interpretation; TCGA‑TCIA datasets supported immunological mechanism exploration, and an interactive prediction platform was developed. Results Only pathological subtype and treatment line exerted clinical predictive effects. The fusion model achieved competitive AUCs: training 0.909, internal validation 0.946, external‑test‑1 0.848, external‑test‑2 0.893. Although standalone 3D DL attained marginally higher AUC in training cohort, fusion outperformed clinical‑only and radiomics‑only models across all cohorts (all P < 0.05). 3D DL features represented the major predictive contributor. The model maintained AUC > 0.87 across most subgroups; calibration and DCA verified favorable consistency and clinical net benefit. SHAP‑Grad‑CAM visualized decision logic, and transcriptomic data associated CT‑defined high‑risk phenotypes with immunosuppressive microenvironments and reduced CD8⁺ T‑cell infiltration. Conclusions This low‑cost interpretable multimodal AI based on routine chest‑CT non‑invasively predicts immunochemotherapy resistance for advanced NSCLC across treatment lines. Validated by two external cohorts, it demonstrates complementary predictive value of radiomic and DL signatures and offers a standardized imaging tool for personalized immunotherapy stratification.

nodes.name: Artificial intelligence‐driven bioinformatics: From analytical pipelines to model‐centered biological discovery
nodes.venue: iMetaOmics
nodes.abstract: Abstract Traditional bioinformatic pipelines, which focus on predefined statistical analyses, are increasingly inadequate for handling high‐dimensional, heterogeneous, and context‐rich multi‐omics, spatial, and clinical datasets. Artificial intelligence (AI) is extending modern bioinformatics from predefined analytical pipelines toward learned biological representations, intervention‐oriented modeling, and more automated discovery workflows. This review comprehensively summarizes AI advances across genomic interpretation, single‐cell and spatial transcriptomics, multi‐omics integration, structural bioinformatics, disease stratification, precision medicine, and drug discovery. We categorize underlying AI technologies, including classical machine learning, deep representation learning, generative foundation models, and executable AI agents, and highlight their complementary use cases alongside inherent limitations and failure modes. Building on rather than claiming priority for the model‐centered paradigm described in recent literature, this review contributes a cross‐domain, failure‐aware evaluation framework organized around six unified axes: representation validity, task‐specific incremental value, robustness under biological and technical distribution shift, causal support, resource requirements, and validation/governance readiness. We further discuss key technical and social barriers and hierarchically prioritize future research directions. We conclude that AI complements rather than replaces conventional bioinformatic tools, extending the capacity for hypothesis generation and mechanism‐driven validation. This review provides structured and practical guidance for robust, interpretable, and clinically translatable AI‐driven biological discovery.

nodes.name: A nomogram model for analyzing risk factors of postpartum hemorrhage in twin pregnancies with cesarean section
nodes.venue: International Journal of Gynecology & Obstetrics
nodes.abstract: Abstract Background The rising prevalence of twin pregnancies and cesarean sections (CS) is a significant risk factor for postpartum hemorrhage (PPH), contributing to increased maternal morbidity and mortality globally. Establishing a reliable risk assessment model for PPH could facilitate timely identification and intervention, thereby improving maternal outcomes. This study aimed to develop an effective nomogram for predicting PPH in twin pregnancies undergoing CS. Methods This retrospective study analyzed data from 1704 women with twin pregnancies who delivered by CS between 2016 and 2022 at the Second Affiliated Hospital of Wenzhou Medical University, China. To identify risk factors for PPH after CS in twin pregnancies, univariate analysis and LASSO (least absolute shrinkage and selection operator) regression were employed. A nomogram was subsequently developed based on the results of binary logistic regression analysis and the Akaike information criterion (AIC). Model validation was performed using bootstrap resampling, with performance assessed through discrimination (receiver operating characteristic curve), calibration (calibration plot and Hosmer‐Lemeshow test), and clinical utility (decision cur analysis, DCA). Results The nomogram for PPH was created using eight best predictor variables, namely, parity, assisted reproductive technology (ART), preeclampsia (PE), placenta previa, placenta accreta, anemia, the sum of the neonatal birthweight, and general anesthesia, which were all independent risk factors for PPH after CS in twin pregnancies. The nomogram demonstrated strong discrimination and calibration performance, with robust clinical utility as evidenced by area under the curve (AUC) analysis and DCA. Internal verification confirmed the consistency between predicted and actual values. Conclusions Parity, the use of ART, PE, placenta previa, placenta accreta, degree of prenatal anemia, total neonatal birthweight, and the use of general anesthesia are significant risk factors affecting the incidence of postpartum hemorrhage after CS in patients. The prediction model based on the above factors provides an accurate tool for assessing PPH risk, offering potential to guide clinical decision‐making and further reduce maternal mortality.
